q: Who is the author of the story "The Necklace"?
o: H. G. Wells
Guy de Maupassant
Ruskin Bond
K. A. Abbas
e: "The Necklace" is written by the French writer Guy de Maupassant. K. A. Abbas wrote "Bholi", Ruskin Bond wrote "The Thief's Story", and H. G. Wells wrote "Footprints Without Feet".

q: Whom was Matilda married to? [JAC PYQ]
o: A wealthy Parisian minister
A famous French merchant
A clerk in Board of Education
A senior military officer
e: Born into a family of clerks with no dowry or prospects, Matilda married M. Loisel, a petty clerk in the office of the Board of Education.

q: Why did Matilda remain unhappy at the beginning of the story? [JAC PYQ]
o: She felt born for luxuries while living modestly
She wanted to leave Paris for a quiet village
Her husband treated her harshly and unkindly
All her former schoolmates treated her with hostility
e: Matilda suffered incessantly because she felt born for all delicacies and luxuries, and resented the poverty of her shabby apartment and worn furniture.

q: Who sent the invitation for the grand ball to M. and Mme Loisel?
o: The Mayor of Paris and his gracious lady
Mme Forestier and her wealthy family in Paris
The President of the Paris Jewellers Association
The Minister of Public Instruction and Mme Ramponneau
e: M. Loisel brought home an invitation from the Minister of Public Instruction and Mme George Ramponneau to an evening reception at the Ministry.

q: On which day and date was the Ministry ball scheduled?
o: Sunday evening, January 10th
Friday evening, February 25th
Monday evening, January 18th
Wednesday evening, March 15th
e: The printed card invited M. and Mme Loisel to the Palace of the Ministry on Monday evening, January 18th.

q: How much money did Matilda ask her husband for buying a suitable dress for the ball?
o: Four hundred francs
Five hundred francs
One thousand francs
Two hundred francs
e: After calculating carefully so her husband would not refuse immediately, Matilda hesitantly asked for four hundred francs.

q: For what purpose had M. Loisel originally saved those four hundred francs?
o: To purchase a diamond ring for his wife
To rent a larger house in central Paris
To pay off an old debt of his father
To buy a gun for summer hunting parties
e: M. Loisel had saved just four hundred francs to buy a gun and join hunting parties on the plain of Nanterre the next summer, yet he gave it to Matilda for her dress.

q: From whom did Matilda borrow the diamond necklace for the ball?
o: Her elder married sister
Her rich friend Mme Forestier
The Minister's gracious wife
Her neighbour's jewellery shop
e: Following her husband's advice, Matilda visited her wealthy schoolmate Mme Forestier and borrowed a diamond necklace from her.

q: In what kind of box was Mme Forestier's diamond necklace kept?
o: A black satin box
A red velvet box
A white leather box
A golden metal box
e: When Matilda asked if she had anything more, Mme Forestier brought out a black satin box containing a superb diamond necklace.

q: Around what time did M. and Mme Loisel leave the Ministry ball?
o: At twelve midnight sharp
At about two in the morning
At about four in the morning
At about six in the morning
e: Matilda danced joyfully all night, and she and her husband finally left the Ministry around four o'clock in the morning.

q: At which place in Paris did the Loisels find an identical replacement diamond necklace?
o: Champs-Élysées
Palais-Royal
Eiffel Tower market
Rue des Martyrs
e: After searching unsuccessfully for a week, the Loisels found a necklace exactly like the lost one in a shop at the Palais-Royal.

q: For how much did the jeweller agree to sell the replacement necklace originally priced at 40,000 francs?
o: Thirty thousand francs
Forty thousand francs
Thirty-five thousand francs
Thirty-six thousand francs
e: Although the necklace was priced at forty thousand francs, the jeweller agreed to let them have it for thirty-six thousand francs.

q: How much money did M. Loisel possess from his father's inheritance to buy the replacement necklace?
o: Ten thousand francs
Eighteen thousand francs
Twelve thousand francs
Twenty-five thousand francs
e: M. Loisel had eighteen thousand francs left to him by his father, and he borrowed the remaining eighteen thousand francs from moneylenders.

q: How many years did it take the Loisels to pay off their entire debt?
o: Five years
Eight years
Ten years
Twelve years
e: Dismissing their maid, living in a garret, and working tirelessly, it took them ten years to repay every bit of the debt with interest.

q: How much was Mme Forestier's original necklace actually worth? [JAC PYQ]
o: Not over five hundred francs
Forty thousand francs exactly
Thirty-six thousand francs exactly
Completely free of cost
e: Ten years later in the Champs-Élysées, Mme Forestier revealed that her original necklace was false (imitation) and not worth over five hundred francs.

q: Who is the author of the story "Bholi"?
o: Ruskin Bond
Victor Canning
Guy de Maupassant
K. A. Abbas
e: "Bholi" is written by Khwaja Ahmad Abbas (K. A. Abbas), portraying the empowerment of a neglected village girl through education.

q: What was Bholi's real name?
o: Champa
Mangla
Radha
Sulekha
e: Bholi's real name was Sulekha, though everyone called her Bholi ("the simpleton") since her childhood accident.

q: What was Bholi's father's name and official position in the village?
o: Numberdar Ramlal, revenue official
Bishamber Nath, wealthy grocer
Master Harilal, school headmaster
Gajadhar Singh, village landlord
e: Bholi's father was Numberdar Ramlal, who served as the village revenue official and government representative.

q: At what age did Sulekha fall off the cot on her head, damaging part of her brain?
o: Ten months old
Two years old
Five years old
Four years old
e: When Sulekha was ten months old, she fell off the cot on her head, perhaps damaging part of her brain and making her a backward child.

q: Which disease attacked Bholi at the age of two, leaving permanent black pockmarks on her body?
o: Severe malaria
Smallpox
Acute cholera
Chronic jaundice
e: At age two, Bholi suffered an attack of smallpox; only her eyes were saved, while her entire body was permanently disfigured by deep black pockmarks.

q: When Bholi finally learnt to speak at the age of five, what speech difficulty did she have?
o: She spoke much too rapidly
She only spoke in whispers
She stammered while speaking
She always sang her words
e: Little Sulekha could not speak till she was five, and when she finally spoke, she stammered, causing other children to mock and mimic her.

q: How many children did Numberdar Ramlal have in all?
o: Four children (two sons, two daughters)
Five children (two sons, three daughters)
Seven children (three sons, four daughters)
Six children (three sons, three daughters)
e: Ramlal had seven children—three sons and four daughters. His sons studied in the city, and Bholi was the youngest of the four daughters.

q: Who came to perform the opening ceremony of the primary school for girls in Bholi's village?
o: The District Magistrate
The Tehsildar Sahib
The village Sarpanch
Bishamber Nath
e: The Tehsildar came to inaugurate the village primary school for girls and urged Ramlal to set an example by sending his daughters to school.

q: What was the name of Ramlal's old cow that had been turned out of the house and sold?
o: Gauri
Nandini
Kamini
Lakshmi
e: Ramlal had turned out and sold their old cow named Lakshmi a few days earlier, so Bholi feared the same fate when her father held her hand.

q: Whose old clean dress was Bholi given to wear on her first day at school?
o: Champa's old dress
Radha's old dress
Mangla's old dress
Her mother's old saree
e: New clothes were never made for Bholi; on her first school day, she received Champa's old clean dress, which had shrunk after many washings.

q: Who comforted Bholi with a soft and soothing voice on her first day at school?
o: The school headmistress
Her classroom teacher
The Tehsildar's wife
Her elder sister Champa
e: When Bholi cried after stammering her name, her teacher spoke in a soft, soothing voice, reassuring her to put fear out of her heart.

q: What was Bishamber Nath's profession?
o: A government schoolteacher
A wealthy landowner farmer
A well-to-do grocer
A railway station master
e: Bishamber Nath was a well-to-do grocer from a neighbouring village who owned a big shop, a house of his own, and several thousand rupees in the bank.

q: How much money did Bishamber Nath demand as dowry upon seeing Bholi's pockmarks? [JAC PYQ]
o: Five thousand rupees
Two thousand rupees
Ten thousand rupees
Twenty thousand rupees
e: Seeing the pockmarks on Bholi's face when her veil slipped back, greedy Bishamber Nath demanded five thousand rupees (Rs. 5,000) from Ramlal to marry her.

q: How much money did Ramlal initially offer Bishamber Nath while placing his turban at his feet?
o: One thousand rupees
Two thousand rupees
Three thousand rupees
Four thousand rupees
e: To save his family's honour, Ramlal placed his turban at Bishamber's feet and begged him to take two thousand rupees, which Bishamber refused.

q: What did Bholi do when Bishamber raised the garland to place it around her neck?
o: She lowered her eyes and wept quietly
She ran inside the house in terror
She bowed down at Bishamber's feet
She flung the garland into the sacred fire
e: Bholi's hand struck out like a streak of lightning, flinging the garland into the fire, and she declared clearly without stammering that she would not marry him.

q: Which simple dinner dish delighted M. Loisel while Matilda dreamed of shining silverware?
o: Roast pheasant
Pot-au-feu / potpie
Pink trout fish
French pastries
e: Uncovering the tureen, M. Loisel would exclaim delightfully over the good potpie (pot-au-feu), whereas Matilda longed for exquisite dinners served on silver.

q: Before thinking of Mme Forestier, what alternative did M. Loisel suggest Matilda wear instead of jewels?
o: Inexpensive silver bracelets
Her mother's pearl chain
Natural roses for ten francs
Velvet and silk ribbons
e: M. Loisel suggested wearing natural flowers, noting two or three magnificent roses cost ten francs, which Matilda rejected as humiliating among rich women.

q: Why did Matilda insist on hurrying away from the Ministry ball at 4 a.m.?
o: Because she suddenly fell ill inside the hall
Because she already saw the necklace had vanished
Because her husband had to reach office early
Because she feared rich ladies seeing her shabby wraps
e: The poverty of the modest wraps M. Loisel put over her shoulders clashed with her ball gown, so she hurried away before women wearing rich furs noticed her.

q: Along which river did the shivering Loisels walk after the ball before finding a night cab?
o: The Seine
The Thames
The Rhine
The Loire
e: Unable to find a carriage at the Ministry door, they walked shivering down toward the Seine until they found one of Paris's old night-prowling cabs.

q: On which Paris street did the Loisels live when they discovered the necklace was missing?
o: Champs-Élysées
Palais-Royal
Rue des Martyrs
Saint-Germain
e: The night cab brought them to their door in the Rue des Martyrs, where Matilda stood before the mirror and discovered the necklace was gone.

q: What excuse did M. Loisel tell Matilda to write to Mme Forestier to buy time?
o: That they had gone out of Paris briefly
That the necklace was stolen and police were searching
That she was having the diamonds cleaned first
That the clasp broke and was being mended
e: To gain time while searching and arranging a replacement, Loisel told Matilda to write that she had broken the clasp and would have it repaired.

q: For how much did the Palais-Royal jeweller agree to buy back the replacement necklace if the original was found before the end of February?
o: Thirty thousand francs
Thirty-two thousand francs
Thirty-four thousand francs
Thirty-six thousand francs
e: The jeweller agreed to take back the replacement necklace for thirty-four thousand francs if the lost one was found before the end of February.

q: During the years of debt, at what rate did M. Loisel do copying work at night?
o: Ten sous a page
Five sous a page
One franc a page
Two sous a page
e: M. Loisel worked in the evenings putting merchants' books in order, and at night he often did copying at five sous a page.

q: What major change in living arrangements did the Loisels make to pay off their debt?
o: Dismissed their maid and rented a small attic
Left Paris completely for a distant village
Sold all furniture and lived in a cheap hotel
Moved into Mme Forestier's spare guest room
e: To survive the debt, the Loisels dismissed their servant, changed their lodgings, and rented modest rooms in an attic.

q: Where did Matilda happen to meet Mme Forestier while taking a Sunday walk ten years later?
o: At Palais-Royal market
Outside the Ministry
On the plain of Nanterre
In the Champs-Élysées
e: One Sunday, while walking in the Champs-Élysées to relax from the cares of the week, Matilda suddenly saw Mme Forestier walking with a child.

q: How did Mme Forestier react when Matilda returned the replacement necklace?
o: Opened the box immediately to inspect the stones
Embraced Matilda warmly and offered a reward
Coldly said it was late, without opening the box
Noticed right away that the diamonds differed
e: Mme Forestier did not open the jewel-box at all and remarked coldly that Matilda should have returned it sooner as she might have needed it.

q: In the sentence "She suffered incessantly, feeling herself born for all delicacies and luxuries," what does "incessantly" mean?
o: Occasionally / rarely
Continuously / non-stop
Secretly / quietly
Suddenly / briefly
e: "Incessantly" means continuously or without interruption, highlighting how Matilda was constantly dissatisfied with her modest lifestyle.

q: In "Matilda waited all day in a state of bewilderment," what state of mind does "bewilderment" describe?
o: Extreme confusion and daze
Deep relief and delight
Fierce anger and revenge
Heavy sleep and laziness
e: "Bewilderment" refers to being utterly confused, dazed, and shocked—Matilda felt completely helpless in the face of the disaster.

q: What was M. Loisel doing while Matilda danced excitedly till 4 a.m. at the ball?
o: He danced enthusiastically with other women at the hall
He stepped outside around midnight to visit a jeweller
He grew tired and went home alone without telling her
He dozed from midnight with three husbands in a side room
e: M. Loisel patiently remained half asleep since midnight in a little deserted room alongside three other husbands whose wives were enjoying themselves.

q: In the story, whom does the word "usurers" refer to?
o: Moneylenders charging high interest
Government income tax inspectors
Experienced Paris night cab drivers
Senior servants in wealthy estates
e: "Usurers" are lenders who charge exorbitant rates of interest; Loisel signed ruinous notes with them to raise the remaining 18,000 francs.

q: What were the names of Bholi's three elder sisters in order from eldest to youngest?
o: Radha, Mangla, Champa
Champa, Mangla, Radha
Mangla, Radha, Champa
Radha, Champa, Mangla
e: According to the text, Radha was the eldest (already married), Mangla was the second (marriage settled), Champa was the third, and Bholi was the fourth.

q: Why was Ramlal's wife initially against sending girls to school?
o: Because monthly school tuition fees were far too high
Because she feared nobody would marry schooled girls
Because the primary school stood miles outside town
Because she needed her daughters for daily farm labour
e: Ramlal's wife held orthodox views and cried, "If girls go to school, who will marry them?"

q: Why did Ramlal's wife finally agree to send Bholi to school?
o: She hoped Bholi would become a respected city teacher
Bholi begged passionately all night to attend classes
Seeing little marriage hope, she left her to the teachers
The Tehsildar promised a cash scholarship for enrolment
e: Unwilling to disobey the Tehsildar yet afraid to spoil her other daughters' prospects, Ramlal's wife suggested sending Bholi since nobody would marry her anyway.

q: Seeing the picture of which animal on the classroom wall reminded Bholi of her family's sold animal?
o: The brown horse
The black goat
The cow like Lakshmi
The green parrot
e: Among the colourful wall pictures (brown horse, black goat, green parrot, and cow), the cow looked just like their family cow Lakshmi.

q: What did the teacher give Bholi at the end of her first day at school?
o: A box of coloured pencils
A book with bright pictures
A brand-new stitched dress
A packet of sweetmeats
e: The teacher gave Bholi a book with bright pictures of animals (dog, cat, goat, horse, parrot, tiger, and a cow like Lakshmi) to encourage her learning.

q: Which developments turned Bholi's village into a small town over the years?
o: High school, tin cinema, cotton mill, and mail-train stop
A sprawling university campus and modern city airport
All village farmlands converted into tall skyscrapers
A large government medical college opened in the centre
e: Over the years, the village grew into a small town: the primary school became a high school, a cinema under a tin shed and a cotton ginning mill opened, and the mail train began stopping at the station.

q: Besides being almost the same age as Ramlal, what else was true about Bishamber Nath?
o: He was completely blind and utterly illiterate
He was deeply poor and crushed by heavy loans
He worked daily as a poor labourer in town
He limped and had grown children from a prior marriage
e: Bishamber Nath was nearly Ramlal's age (forty-five or fifty), walked with a limp, and had grown-up children from his first wife.

q: Why did Bishamber Nath initially agree to marry Bholi without asking for dowry?
o: He was an idealistic reformer opposing all dowry
Being from another village, he didn't know of her scars
He deeply admired Bholi's high-school education
Ramlal promised to gift him half his agricultural land
e: Ramlal's wife noted that since Bishamber was from another village, he knew nothing about Bholi's pockmarks and supposed lack of sense.

q: How did Bishamber Nath arrive at Ramlal's house on the wedding day?
o: Quietly in an ordinary bullock cart with two relatives
On a decorated horse with a baraat and brass band
Walking modestly in plain clothes with his two sons
Riding inside an official jeep alongside the Tehsildar
e: Bishamber arrived with a big party of friends and relatives, a brass band playing a popular Indian film tune, and riding a decorated horse.

q: Who slipped back the silken veil from Bholi's face just before the garland ceremony?
o: Bishamber Nath himself
Bholi herself in anger
One of the women standing nearby
The priest performing the ritual
e: Just as Bishamber lifted the garland of yellow marigolds, a woman slipped back the silken veil from Bholi's face, revealing her pockmarks.

q: How did Ramlal respond when Bishamber demanded Rs. 5,000 at the wedding?
o: Put his turban at his feet, begged, and paid Rs. 5,000
Ordered Bishamber and the entire party out at once
Went straight to the police station to file a complaint
Told Bholi to reject the greedy groom immediately
e: With tears streaming down his face, Ramlal put his turban at Bishamber's feet; when two thousand was rejected, he brought five thousand rupees from his safe.

q: Why did the confused bandsmen strike up a closing song at the end of the scene?
o: Because all wedding rituals had ended happily
Because Ramlal paid them extra cash to play it
Because midnight had struck and hours ended
Seeing the baraat leave, they assumed it ended
e: As Bishamber Nath turned back with his party after Bholi's refusal, the confused bandsmen assumed the wedding was over and played a closing song.

q: How did Sulekha (Bholi) reassure her grieving father after the wedding broke off?
o: She would move away to a city degree college
She would look for a kind, educated husband
She would serve parents and teach at her school
She would join the village cotton ginning mill
e: Sulekha told Ramlal in a calm, steady voice not to worry—she would serve him and Mother in their old age and teach in the same school.

q: What does the description of Ramlal as a "numberdar" and "prosperous farmer" indicate about his household?
o: The family suffered severe poverty and debt
He had village standing and ample food at home
They lived outside the village in a mud hut
They owned no farmland or cattle
e: As Numberdar and a prosperous farmer, Ramlal enjoyed social standing and plenty of food at home, making his neglect of Bholi even starker.

q: What is the exact meaning of "contemptible" as used by Bholi for Bishamber ("mean, greedy and contemptible coward")?
o: Worthy of great respect and honour
Extremely innocent and forgiving
Very courageous and generous
Despicable / deserving utter scorn
e: "Contemptible" means deserving contempt or scorn—Bholi used it to expose Bishamber's shameless greed and cowardice at the wedding.

q: Dialogue Analysis: When Matilda tossed the invitation spitefully onto the table saying, "What do you suppose I want with that?", what trait does this reveal?
o: Her vanity outweighed gratitude for her husband's thoughtful effort
She felt deeply anxious around unfamiliar guests at formal receptions
She secretly feared falling ill before the grand January reception
She wanted her husband to go alone and lobby the Minister for a raise
e: Instead of appreciating her husband's pride and effort in securing the prestigious invite, Matilda reacted petulantly because her vanity felt threatened without an expensive gown.

q: Cause-Effect: Why did Matilda weep for whole days after returning from visits to her convent friend Mme Forestier?
o: Because Mme Forestier openly ridiculed Matilda's shabby everyday attire
Comparing her friend's luxury with her own modest life deepened her despair
Because fond school memories left her bitterly nostalgic for carefree youth
Because her husband strongly discouraged future visits to wealthy households
e: Seeing Mme Forestier's affluence reminded Matilda painfully of everything she lacked, leaving her consumed by envy, disappointment, and self-pity.

q: Character Contrast: How did M. Loisel's priorities differ from Matilda's regarding the 400 francs?
o: Loisel gave up hunting for her joy; Matilda put vanity first
Both husband and wife felt equally reluctant to spend any savings
Loisel flatly refused her request and bought his hunting rifle instead
Matilda urged keeping every franc safely for household emergencies
e: Although he turned slightly pale at losing his hunting plan, M. Loisel unselfishly gave up his savings to make Matilda happy, contrasting with her self-absorption.

q: Extract Inference: "She waited all day in a state of bewilderment before this frightful disaster." What does this show about Matilda during the crisis?
o: She believed the missing diamond necklace would turn up indoors
She had already visited Mme Forestier to confess the loss early
She froze helplessly while M. Loisel led the entire frantic search
She felt emotionally detached from losing her friend's borrowed jewel
e: While M. Loisel walked the cold streets at 7 a.m., visited the police, cab offices, and newspapers, Matilda remained paralyzed at home in bewilderment.

q: Plot Analysis: What crucial omission right after losing the necklace sealed the Loisels' ten-year fate?
o: They failed to inspect cheaper jewellers beyond the Palais-Royal shops
They forgot to inform the police station or place newspaper notices
M. Loisel delayed withdrawing the inheritance left by his father
Matilda hid the truth, and Mme Forestier never opened the jewel-box
e: Because Matilda's pride kept her silent and Mme Forestier did not open the box upon return, neither realized they had replaced false paste with real diamonds.

q: Cause-Effect: Why did Matilda rush down the stairs into the street instead of waiting inside for a cab after the ball?
o: Because the cool dawn air outside felt refreshing after a crowded dance
Her pride dreaded wealthy ladies spotting her humble wraps
Because the Ministry guards asked lingering guests to leave promptly
Because they had to catch an early morning train from Paris
e: Having dazzled everyone at the ball, Matilda's vanity dreaded being seen in her shabby everyday wraps by wealthy ladies—and in that rush, the necklace was lost.

q: Character Evolution: What irony lies in Matilda becoming "the woman of impoverished households—strong and hard and rough"?
o: Years of toil turned her secretly richer and more influential than before
High society began praising her modest attire and hardworking lifestyle
The beauty she flaunted for one night was ruined by that debt
She avoided all household labour and spent the decade in idle daydreaming
e: Her desire to showcase her beauty for one glamorous night triggered a decade of harsh drudgery that ruined her delicate looks, turning her coarse and aged.

q: Dialogue Interpretation: When M. Loisel cried, "How stupid we are! Go and find your friend Mme Forestier...", what motivated him?
o: To embarrass Matilda in front of her wealthy convent schoolmate
To ask Mme Forestier for a cash loan alongside the dress
To discourage Matilda from attending the Ministry ball altogether
Finding a cost-free way for Matilda to wear fine jewels
e: Having already spent his savings on the dress, Loisel genuinely wanted Matilda to feel confident at the ball and saw borrowing from her close friend as an easy solution.

q: Theme Application: Which proverb best applies to Matilda's mistake in the first half of the story?
o: Cut your coat according to your cloth (live within means)
A single careless mistake always ruins an entire lifetime
Look before you leap, yet leisurely ease always comes first
Where there is a will, effortless shortcuts always appear
e: Matilda's refusal to accept her modest reality and her desire to appear far wealthier than her means directly brought about her financial and personal ruin.

q: Extract Analysis: Why did Matilda address Mme Forestier informally as "Good morning, Jeanne" ten years later?
o: She wanted to embarrass Mme Forestier publicly in the park
After repaying every franc honestly, she felt quiet pride
She wished to test whether her old friend remembered her childhood name
She came intending to borrow another expensive jewel for a party
e: Having paid off the entire debt through honest toil, Matilda no longer felt inferior or guilty; she approached Jeanne with quiet dignity and self-respect.

q: Cause-Effect: Why could Mme Forestier not recognize Matilda at first in the Champs-Élysées?
o: Because Matilda wore dark glasses and a thick winter hat
Because the two women had never actually met face to face before
Because ten hard years of poverty had aged Matilda completely
Because advancing age had severely weakened Mme Forestier's eyesight
e: Exhausting chores, rough living, and a decade of deprivation had transformed the once-radiant Matilda into an aged, coarse-looking working woman.

q: Character Judgment: What quality of M. Loisel stands out when he spends his 18,000-franc inheritance and signs ruinous loan notes?
o: A reckless habit of taking foolish financial gambles without thinking
Constant terror of immediate police arrest and courtroom trials
A desire to impress the Palais-Royal jeweller with his wealth
Selfless devotion to Matilda and integrity to honour debt
e: Even though borrowing ruined his financial future, M. Loisel never blamed Matilda and honourably dedicated a decade of toil to repaying every penny.

q: Extract Interpretation: Why does the narrator describe Matilda as "intoxicated with pleasure" at the ball?
o: For one evening she won the admiration she always craved
She had consumed excessive wine at the royal Ministry banquet
The Minister had just promised a high promotion to her husband
Mme Forestier had secretly gifted her the necklace during the evening
e: Surrounded by admiring men, Cabinet attachés wanting to dance, and the Minister's praise, Matilda was swept away by the social triumph she had long fantasized about.

q: Counterfactual Reasoning: If the Loisels had confessed the loss to Mme Forestier immediately, what would most likely have happened?
o: Mme Forestier would have called the police right away
They would learn it was paste worth under 500 francs
The jeweller would have donated real diamonds out of pity
M. Loisel would lose his Education Board post immediately
e: Had they been honest from the start, Mme Forestier would have told them the jewels were paste worth at most 500 francs, sparing them ten years of hardship.

q: Vocabulary in Context: What does "triumph" signify in "forgetting everything in the triumph of her beauty"?
o: Deep quiet shame and bitter embarrassment
Heavy exhaustion and dull boredom
Complete victory and proud success
Unnecessary anger toward other guests
e: "Triumph" here conveys a glorious victory or crowning success, capturing Matilda's pride in outshining every other woman at the reception.

q: Extract Inference: Why did Bholi believe she was going to a better place only after being bathed, oiled, and given a clean dress?
o: Because her father bought her a brand-new leather schoolbag
Because Champa affectionately gave her festive sweets outside
Because village children cheered loudly at the courtyard gate
Because nobody had ever cared for her appearance before
e: Always neglected in tattered clothes, Bholi had never been bathed or oiled with care before; this sudden attention convinced her she was not being abandoned.

q: Character Analysis: Why did Sulekha (Bholi) talk very little during her childhood?
o: Because other children mocked and mimicked her stammer
Because she preferred quietly reading storybooks alone in a corner
Because Ramlal strictly forbade her from speaking before guests
Because speaking caused her intense physical throat pain
e: Because other children mocked and mimicked her stammer, Bholi withdrew into silence and talked very little to avoid humiliation.

q: Cause-Effect: Why did Ramlal feel unable to refuse the Tehsildar's advice despite his wife's strong opposition?
o: The Tehsildar was Ramlal's closest family relative nearby
As Numberdar, Ramlal dared not disobey a revenue superior
The government awarded generous cash grants to families
Ramlal held deeply progressive views on female schooling
e: As a government revenue official (Numberdar), Ramlal was expected to set a village example and told his wife he lacked the courage to disobey the Tehsildar.

q: Symbolic Meaning: What did Bholi's feeling that "all the bells in the village temple were ringing" and "the trees had blossomed into big red flowers" signify?
o: An annual temple festival had just started in the village
Morning prayers ended and the school recess bell had rung
Her teacher's kindness awakened new hope and joy inside her
Bright red spring blossoms opened across the school courtyard
e: For the first time in her life, someone spoke to her gently and promised respect instead of ridicule, filling Bholi's heart with joy and a new lease on life.

q: Social Inference: Why were Bholi's elder sisters envious of her luck upon seeing Bishamber's wedding procession?
o: Bishamber appeared remarkably young, handsome, and refined
Bholi had already completed an advanced college diploma
Bishamber gifted expensive gold jewellery to every sister
Society equated a groom's wealth and pomp with good luck

Poor rural road networks and delayed rail connections

Rapid industrial growth of synthetic glass manufacturing in France
Professional honesty and fair pricing among Parisian jewellers
The natural superiority of sparkling gems over simple roses
e: Even wealthy Mme Forestier wore paste diamonds—proving that society's glittering facade is often an illusion lacking real substance.

q: Comparative Competency (Matilda vs Bholi): How do Matilda's and Bholi's attitudes toward social opinion fundamentally contrast?
o: Both women sacrificed happiness fearing idle village gossip
Bholi shared Matilda's intense craze for jewels and finery
Matilda chased elites; Bholi rejected false "izzat"
Matilda rebelled loudly while Bholi submitted calmly forever
e: Matilda becomes a victim of her obsession with social appearances, whereas educated Bholi shatters oppressive social expectations to protect her self-worth.

q: Competency Inference: "But sometimes, when her husband was at the office, she would seat herself before the window and think of that evening party..." What does this reveal about Matilda?
o: She schemed to borrow another diamond jewel right away
Even after ruin, she still cherished that brief triumph
She felt bitter anger over M. Loisel's modest earnings
She plotted to sue the Palais-Royal jeweller for cash
e: Even after hardships altered her, Matilda still looked back wistfully on her one night of triumph—capturing Maupassant's nuanced portrait of human desire.

q: Authorial Craft: Why does Maupassant end the story abruptly right after Mme Forestier's revelation without showing Matilda's reply?
o: Because the author simply ran out of plot ideas for a final chapter
Because the two friends immediately broke into a bitter argument
Because Mme Forestier had to hurry home before evening rain began
To let the shock of ten wasted years hit readers hard
e: Cutting off at the revelation leaves readers stunned by the devastating irony of ten lost years, making any further dialogue unnecessary.

q: Social Critique: What does Mme Forestier casually owning a 500-franc imitation necklace suggest about Parisian high society?
o: Rich elites also wore cheap imitations to keep up status
Real diamonds were strictly outlawed across nineteenth-century Paris
Mme Forestier was notoriously stingy toward every childhood friend
Only clerks' wives possessed the training to spot real diamonds
e: While Matilda ruined her life assuming her rich friend's jewels were priceless, the elite themselves cheerfully wore fakes to maintain status.

q: Critical Thinking: What mistake in Matilda's sense of value is exposed when she rejects fresh natural roses?
o: She had suffered severe physical allergies to flower pollen since childhood
She was too stingy to spend even ten francs on evening accessories
She feared real roses would wither before reaching the Ministry hall
She valued costly display far above natural simplicity
e: Instead of appreciating natural beauty and modesty, Matilda believed only costly gems could earn her respect among elite women.

q: Competency Chain (CBSE PYQ): Which sequence demonstrates how "one little act of negligence" combined with vanity led to total ruin?
o: Getting the invite → buying a gown → riding near the Seine
Losing the jewel → hiding truth → buying costly diamonds
Dismissing the maid → renting an attic → strolling on Sundays
Opening the box → dancing till 4 a.m. → waking up around noon
e: A careless rush caused the loss, while vanity prevented honest inquiry or verification—compounding one mistake into ten years of financial ruin.

q: Character Nuance: Which assessment best describes Mme Forestier's character across the whole story?
o: Cruel and scheming, deliberately trapping her old classmate
Deeply envious of Matilda's happy marriage to an honest clerk
Brief on return, yet generous and deeply moved at the end
Fully aware of the swap, yet greedy enough to remain quiet
e: She lent her jewel willingly, returned it to storage without checking, and cried out in genuine horror and pity when she learnt Matilda's truth.

q: Moral Takeaway: Which life lesson best captures Maupassant's message in "The Necklace"?
o: Contentment and honesty guard life against hollow vanity
One must never lend or borrow anything even from close childhood friends
Attending formal social gatherings and public receptions should be avoided
Accumulating vast wealth is the only reliable path to social respect
e: Through Matilda's tragedy, Maupassant warns that chasing false status breeds misery, whereas honesty and contentment preserve peace and dignity.

q: Narrative Tone: How does the narrator's tone toward Matilda evolve from the beginning to the final third of the story?
o: From blind admiration at first to bitter scorn at the end
From light comedy to dry notes on nineteenth-century politics
Unchanging, harsh moral condemnation across every single scene
From irony at her snobbery to quiet empathy for her grit
e: While opening with subtle irony at Matilda's snobbery, the narrator portrays her decade of uncomplaining endurance with genuine respect and pathos.

q: Irony of Names: What is the profound irony between the nickname "Bholi" and Sulekha's final stand at the wedding?
o: After halting the match, she demanded people call her Bholi
Mocked as foolish, she proved far wiser than her elders
Bishamber Nath too was mocked as foolish throughout his youth
Her teacher officially renamed her Lakshmi on the very first day
e: While the "wise" elders bowed to greed and false pride, the girl dismissed as a simpleton demonstrated true intelligence and moral strength.

q: Thematic Competency: How does K.A. Abbas show that real education goes far beyond merely reading and writing?
o: True education nurtures dignity and courage against evil
The sole practical purpose of educating girls is reducing dowry demands
Schooling inevitably alienates young women from their parents and villages
Literacy adds little value compared to inheriting family wealth
e: Education didn't merely teach Bholi to read; it cured her fear, sharpened her sense of justice, and enabled her to reject humiliation and support her parents.

q: Moral Contrast: Contrast Ramlal's understanding of "izzat" (honour) with Bholi's understanding at the wedding mandap.
o: Ramlal valued his cash savings while Bholi urged him to pay higher dowry
Bholi judged family prestige purely by the grandeur of the wedding band
Father and daughter held the exact same traditional definition of honour
Ramlal feared village gossip; Bholi defended self-respect
e: Ramlal sacrificed self-respect at Bishamber's feet fearing village gossip, while Bholi proved true honour lies in refusing exploitation.

q: Symbolic Parallel: Why does the author include the episode of the cow Lakshmi early on and echo it when an old woman calls Bholi a "dumb cow" at the wedding?
o: Society treated girls like cattle until education freed Bholi
It proves Bholi secretly dreamed of running her father's dairy farm
Both scenes fondly celebrate rural villagers' care for gentle pets
Bishamber asked Ramlal to gift a healthy milch cow alongside rupees
e: The parallel between selling old Lakshmi and handing Bholi over to an exploitative groom underscores how education freed her from being treated as helpless property.

q: Critical Analysis: Why did Bholi call Bishamber specifically a "contemptible coward" in addition to "mean" and "greedy"?
o: Because he panicked at barking village dogs down the lane
Because he cornered a helpless father in public for money
Because he tried to flee quietly without paying his bandsmen
Because he stumbled while dismounting his decorated horse
e: Exploiting a vulnerable father in public when he assumed the bride's family had no choice left was an act of sheer moral cowardice.

q: Social Satire: What social flaw is satirized through Bholi's sisters envying her "luck" at the sight of Bishamber's grand baraat?
o: Elder sisters naturally resent the good fortune of younger siblings
Playing brass bands and cinema songs spoils traditional wedding dignity
Society judges matches by pomp, ignoring character and age
Arriving on a decorated horse brings misfortune to the bride's family
e: The sisters' envy exposes how glittering wedding displays blind people to profound mismatches in age, respect, and moral character.

q: Pedagogical Insight: Why was the teacher's gentle command, "Put the fear out of your heart," the decisive turning point in curing Bholi's stammer?
o: The teacher secretly gave her herbal medicine for her voice
No other schoolgirl in that classroom was permitted to speak aloud
Bholi stopped speaking completely at home for several silent months
Fear caused her stammer; gentle reassurance unlocked her voice
e: Ridicule at home and among peers deepened her anxiety; gentle encouragement and a respectful environment freed her from fear, letting her speak fluently.

q: Literary Metaphor: Comparing the teacher to "an artist contemplating her masterpiece" suggests what ideal about teaching?
o: A true teacher patiently shapes a fearful child into strength
Teachers must always attend every pupil's family wedding party
Every rural schoolteacher ought to earn a formal fine-arts degree
Teachers, like painters, should focus purely on gifted pupils
e: Just as an artist shapes raw material with patience and vision, Bholi's teacher transformed a broken, neglected girl into a courageous young woman.

q: Character Contrast: Compare Bholi's silence on Day 1 at school with Sulekha's calm demeanour at the end of the story.
o: In both scenes she felt equally defeated, nervous, and hopeless
At the end she stayed mute because shock brought back her stammer
Day 1's silence came from fear; her final calm shows inner strength
She acted stubbornly proud on Day 1 and deeply humbled at the end
e: On Day 1 she shrank into a corner in panic; at the end, her calm and steady voice consoles her grieving father with a clear vision for her future.

q: Competency Reasoning (CBSE PYQ): Why did Sulekha choose to "teach in the same school" rather than passively wait for another marriage match?
o: She felt terrified of ever stepping outside her familiar village
To earn, care for parents, and empower other village girls
Ramlal strictly forbade his daughter from leaving the village
Every other teacher at the high school had suddenly resigned
e: Teaching gives Sulekha economic self-reliance, enables her to care for her parents respectfully, and lets her uplift future generations of girls.

q: Critical Evaluation: What sharp contradiction is seen in Ramlal's parenting of his sons versus his daughters?
o: He sent daughters to college while keeping sons on the farm
He sent all seven children equally to city boarding schools
He educated his sons in town yet neglected girls' schooling
Being unlettered, he opposed education for sons and girls alike
e: Despite being prosperous, Ramlal reserved higher education in the city exclusively for his sons while viewing daughters solely through the lens of marriage.

q: Symbolic Interpretation: What does "the flames of the sacred fire slowly died down" symbolize near the end of the story?
o: An unexpected evening storm extinguishing the courtyard flames
Damp firewood carelessly piled by Ramlal for the wedding ritual
The permanent darkening of all Bholi's future hopes and safety
The end of a greedy match and start of Sulekha's free life
e: The dying flames mark the end of a transaction built on greed and false honour, clearing the ground for Sulekha's independent and dignified new beginning.

q: Comparative Competency: Contrast the impact of Mme Forestier on Matilda with the impact of the teacher on Bholi.
o: Forestier's jewel fed vanity; Bholi's teacher sparked freedom
Both mentors pushed the protagonists into decades of severe want
Both advised that outer glamour outweighs quiet inner integrity
Mme Forestier proved selfless while Bholi's teacher sought gain
e: Bholi's teacher empowers her from within through compassion and learning, while Matilda's borrowed glamour from Mme Forestier deepens her entrapment in vanity.

q: Societal Psychology: Why did the wedding guests tolerate Bishamber's Rs. 5,000 extortion in silence, yet immediately brand Bholi "shameless" when she protested?
o: Because Bishamber promised guests a share of his Rs. 5,000 cash
Because guests felt Rs. 5,000 meant little to wealthy Ramlal
Patriarchal bias excused male greed while shaming female courage
Because village tradition forbade brides from uttering any word
e: Traditional bias pardoned a wealthy groom's public extortion as acceptable bargaining, while demonizing a young woman simply for refusing humiliation.

q: Chapter Synthesis ("The Necklace" & "Bholi"): Reading both stories together, which shared overarching message emerges for Class 10 students?
o: Social prestige requires displaying expensive attire regardless of cost
Conventional marriage at any price remains the only guarantee of security
Long-standing poverty and social prejudice can never be challenged successfully
True worth lies in honesty, education, and quiet dignity
e: Matilda's downfall warns against vanity and dishonesty, while Bholi's triumph proves that education and self-respect empower individuals to defeat social injustice.
